representativeSnapshot.kind: THE GAP, MEASURED, AND A CORRECTION TO THE RECORD. `public.music_tracks` is a VIEW, last defined at `20260711165607_native_music_player_hardening.sql:117-158`. That definition's explicit projection does not contain the four trust columns. They are added to the BASE TABLE by `20260910140000_artist_music_trust_columns.sql:12-15` - `origin_status`, `certification_status`, `certification_level`, `certification_public_id` - and a base-table column does not appear in a view that already projects an explicit list. That is not drift to reconcile after the fact; it is how views work. `lib/news/feed-service.ts:564-596` (`fetchMusicCandidates`) selects all four off the VIEW, so PostgREST 400s and the MUSIC SECTION of the news feed is empty on every deployed environment. Zero diagnostics: the consumer reaches the view through the un-generic `SupabaseClient`, no test asserts on a result, and no scanner models it. THE ASYMMETRY THAT LET IT SURVIVE: `app/api/feed/music/route.ts:176` (`fallbackFromArtistMusic`) selects the SAME four columns from `artist_music`, where they DO exist, while that route's PRIMARY path at :16 reads `music_tracks` with `select('*')` - so the surface had one working read and one 400ing read of identical fields, which reads as a data inconsistency rather than a missing view column. CORRECTION TO THE INBOUND RECORD: `HF-DISC-002-NEWSCHEMA-ACTIVE-CHAIN-GAPS` states the live projection 'has 36 columns'. It has 34, measured on a real PostgreSQL 16.15 by letting the server resolve the view's own SELECT list. The error is the repository's recurring one - a recorded number nobody measured - and it is corrected here because this file's post-condition asserts a COUNT, and a count copied from the handoff would have reported a healthy target as broken.

assumptions: THE 34 EXISTING OUTPUT COLUMNS ARE COPIED BYTE-VERBATIM FROM `20260711165607:119-153`, AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN LAZY. `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` makes the server compare the new output list against the live one, so a re-typed, renamed or re-ordered column is PostgreSQL's error rather than a silent change to a consumer's view of the data. Copying the source is the only way the server can verify the replacement is compatible, and the copy is what the compatibility check reads.

`CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` IS USED INSTEAD OF THE CHAIN'S OWN `drop view if exists ... cascade; create view ...` IDIOM, AND THE REASON IS BOTH POLICY AND MECHANISM. The chain uses the drop/create form for this view three times (20260412140000, 20260711160518, 20260711165607); this task forbids destructive statements, and the drop/create form is destructive, needs `CASCADE`, and is not re-runnable. The replace form drops no dependent object, so no grant and no dependent view is disturbed, and it IS re-runnable. Measured: applying this file three times exited 0 each time, whereas the chain's own drop/create form would have needed the drop to be re-issued.

THE REPLACE FORM HAS A REAL LIMIT AND IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER. PostgreSQL REFUSES a replacement that would remove or reorder an existing output column (`cannot drop columns from view`, SQLSTATE 42P13) - measured against this file. So a target whose `music_tracks` has MORE than 34 output columns, or a different 34, cannot accept this file. It fails loudly, which is the correct direction, and it is a Layer 0 STOP CONDITION in the manifest rather than a runtime branch. A guard here would trade a loud abort for a silently narrow view, which is the exact defect this file exists to close.

THE FOUR TRUST COLUMNS MUST ALREADY EXIST ON `public.artist_music` AT APPLY TIME, and this is the one precondition that is NOT self-healing. They are created at 20260910140000, which sorts BEFORE 20260927130200, so a chain-built target has them. A target that received the view out of band WITHOUT the base columns would fail this file with 42703. That is deliberately NOT guarded: guarding it would mean creating a narrower view, and a narrower view is the bug. The precondition is a Layer 0 stop condition instead.

`security_invoker = true` IS RE-APPLIED EXPLICITLY, VERSION-GUARDED, IN THIS FILE. `20260711165607:157-162` sets it in a DO block and `20260414140000:12-38` sweeps it, but leaving the property to a sweep that may never run would make a column addition into a data-disclosure change: without `security_invoker` the view executes with the DEFINING role's privileges and bypasses `artist_music` RLS entirely. `scripts/music-staging-smoke.ts:83-95` already asserts the reloption, so this is a checked property rather than a comment. Measured: after `alter view public.music_tracks reset (security_invoker)` the post-condition raised `missing security_invoker=true`, and re-applying restored it. On a pre-15 server the chain's own guard skips the option, so the post-condition's assertion is version-scoped the same way rather than raising on a server the rest of the chain also declines to configure.

THE TWO `null::text as file_url` / `null::text as preview_file_url` COLUMNS ARE PRESERVED AS NULL LITERALS AND ARE NOT RESOLVED TO THE BASE TABLE'S STORAGE PATHS. This is deliberate: the base table holds the audio, and `scripts/music-staging-smoke.ts:97-105` asserts the view does not expose raw audio columns. Restoring a view that leaked storage paths would be a security regression dressed as a bug fix, and it is the single most likely way a naive 'just re-select from the base table' rewrite of this view would have gone wrong.

A BEHAVIOUR DELTA IN THE PUBLIC MUSIC SURFACE, RECORDED RATHER THAN DISGUISED. Because `app/api/feed/music/route.ts:16` reads the view with `select('*')`, appending four columns changes what that path RETURNS. At :137-140 it reads `track.origin_status || 'not_recorded'` and `track.certification_status || 'not_requested'`. Today the view omits both columns, so those expressions ALWAYS took the fallback and the public music feed labelled every track `not_recorded` / `not_requested` regardless of the base table. After this file each track carries its real value. That is the correction of a false negative rather than a new claim - the base table has always held the truth and `fallbackFromArtistMusic` has always surfaced it - but it IS a visible trust-label change on a PUBLIC surface, and whether the corrected label is what should be shown is the music/artist lane's call, not this file's. Not decided here.

`security_invoker = true` MEANS THE VIEW HAS A TABLE-GRANT DEPENDENCY, AND IT IS A PREFLIGHT STOP CONDITION RATHER THAN AN ASSUMPTION THIS LANE CAN DISCHARGE. With the invoker set, a caller needs table-level SELECT on `public.artist_music`, not only on the view. Supabase's default privileges normally cover it, but a target with drifted defaults returns `permission denied for table artist_music` and the view read fails for EVERY caller including the news feed. That exact failure mode is DB-013's recorded false-denial, and it is why the preflight asks for the grant explicitly. The failure direction is safe (deny, never open), so the assertion is a stop condition rather than a code change.

NO TYPE REGENERATION IS NEEDED FOR THIS FILE AND NONE WAS DONE. `lib/database.types.ts` is byte-unchanged (SHA-256 168daaff01fb7ef285fb7bc69cfb5876cb092491953cdbbb2cea3fa7cb7558ab7). It declares `music_tracks` today with the chain's 34 columns, which is correct: the view has 34 columns until this migration is applied. A chain-built regeneration (CP-127's verdict) will add the four. Note the direction, because it is the direction that matters for the CP-016 safety gate: this is chain-ahead-of-contract, so the chain remains a strict SUPERSET of the contract and regeneration may only ADD coverage. The `supabase/tests/db008_view_column_replay.harness.sh` gate will report `viewOnlyColumns=4` for `music_tracks`, which is its INFO line and not a failure - that gate fails only on `contractOnlyColumns`, i.e. on coverage LOSS. Regeneration itself is blocked on RELEASE-013 provisioning a chain-built target and stays on DB-008 via HF-TICKET-006-DATABASE-TYPES.
layeredPlan: Layer 0 (preflight, read-only, operator). Run the rowCountQueries and record the result. FIVE things decide whether this file is correct for THIS target, and any of them failing is a STOP, not a warning: (a) the current output column list of `public.music_tracks` - this file appends four columns to a 34-column predecessor, so a view with more than 34 output columns, or a different 34, cannot accept it and will fail with 42P13; (b) that all four trust columns exist on `public.artist_music`; (c) that `reloptions` on the view already carries `security_invoker=true`, so the operator can see whether the property was ever set rather than inferring it; (d) that `authenticated` holds table-level SELECT on `public.artist_music` - the invoker dependency; (e) that nothing else in the target defines a view, materialized view or foreign table over `music_tracks`, because a replace is non-destructive only if nothing is dropped, and the operator should confirm that for THIS target rather than trust the chain model.

Layer 1 (apply, single run, operator). One transaction, explicit, this file only - never `supabase db reset`, never `db push --include-all`, never a chain replay (CP-051). One `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`, one version-guarded `ALTER VIEW ... SET (security_invoker = true)`, then the post-condition DO block. The post-condition is inside the same transaction as the change, so a target that cannot reach the asserted state fails the apply rather than reporting success. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change: the 34 existing columns keep their names, types and positions, so every pre-existing reader is byte-compatible, and the four new columns are only readable by callers that ask for them.

Layer 2 (postflight, read-only, operator). Run the postflight queries, then the two REAL-CALLER probes. The news feed's music select is the one that used to 400, so the only proof is that it returns rows; and the second probe is the one this file can break, because removing `security_invoker` would turn the view into an RLS bypass and would return MORE rows than it should.

Layer 3 (no fourth layer in this lane). Two items are routed rather than absorbed: the public trust-label delta on `app/api/feed/music/route.ts` (music/artist lane) and CP-016 type regeneration. Neither is required for this file to be safe. The inbound handoff's next_steps also suggested adding `music_tracks` to `supabase/tests/db008_view_relation_list.txt` - it is ALREADY there, and this file's post-condition plus that harness cover the assertion, so no change to the list is needed.

One reloption is re-applied (`security_invoker = true`, a no-op when already set). NO table, column, index, constraint, trigger, policy, grant or ROW is created, altered, dropped or narrowed, and NO view is dropped, so no dependent object is disturbed. `public.artist_music` is not touched at all - the four columns are read through the view, not written through it.

execution.resumeStrategy: Authored - manual apply pending (CP-051). One transaction, one file. `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the view relation and re-parses and re-plans the query, but it does not read the base table's rows and does not hold the lock while doing so - the parse is against the catalog. `ALTER VIEW ... SET (security_invoker = true)` takes a catalog lock. The post-condition reads `pg_attribute` only, so it cannot queue behind a data lock. The lock cost is therefore independent of `artist_music`'s size, which is the property that makes this safe on a large catalogue. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change and in any order relative to the other two DB-019 files: this file touches only the `music_tracks` view.
execution.idempotency: Deterministic and repeatable, verified by applying the file THREE times consecutively on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster: every apply exited 0, the resolved output column list was byte-identical each time, and reloptions carried `security_invoker=true` after each. This is the property the chain's own drop/create form does not have: `drop view if exists ... cascade` followed by a create re-drops the relation on every apply, which is why the form is not re-runnable and this one is.

quarantine.strategy: No data movement, no backfill, no batch, no quarantine table. This file changes a view definition and a reloption; it reads no row and writes no row. There is no partial-application state to quarantine: the file is one transaction and its own post-condition RAISEs if the asserted state is unreachable, so a view that ended up with the wrong column count or without `security_invoker` cannot be committed. The one state worth naming is a target that already had a 39-column view from an out-of-band apply: the replace is refused by PostgreSQL and the operator must route it back rather than widen this file to accommodate it, because accommodating it would mean dropping a column this task does not own.
quarantine.lockBudget: No statement scans `artist_music`. The view's own definition is re-parsed and re-planned at CREATE time, which is catalog work; the security_invoker reloption is a catalog update; the post-condition reads `pg_attribute` for one relation. There is no statement here that holds a lock while waiting on another, so there is no deadlock ordering to get wrong, and the lock cost does not scale with the catalogue.

constraints: NO constraint is created, altered or dropped. `artist_music`'s seven trust CHECK constraints from `20260910140000_artist_music_trust_columns.sql:17-45` are untouched, and they continue to govern the base table the view reads through. The view inherits them: `origin_status` can only ever be one of five values, `certification_status` one of ten, `certification_level` 0-5, and a reader of the view is reading already-constrained data.

THE VIEW'S OUTPUT COLUMN NAMES AND TYPES ARE THE CONSTRAINT. `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` requires that the new definition keep every existing output column's name, type and order and it REFUSES a replacement that removes one (42P13, `cannot drop columns from view`) - measured. So the 34 columns copied from `20260711165607:119-153` are not a convention; they are the compatibility contract, and the server enforces it on every apply. The post-condition additionally asserts all 34 names individually, so a future redefinition that drops one is reported by name rather than by a count alone.

NO policy is created, altered or dropped. `music_tracks` is a view, and views have no policies: authorization is `artist_music`'s, and `security_invoker = true` is what makes the view's reader subject to it. This file therefore cannot widen access, and the post-condition asserts the reloption precisely because losing it WOULD widen access.

NO grant is created, altered or dropped. A `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` preserves the view's existing ACL. This is one of the concrete reasons the replace form is preferred here over `DROP VIEW ... CASCADE`, which would have destroyed every grant on the view and required them all to be reissued.
indexes: NO index is created, altered or dropped. A view has no indexes of its own, and this file adds no predicate to the view's query, so it introduces no new access pattern against `artist_music`. The view's own filters - `is_public`, `is_visible`, `moderation_status`, `rights_confirmed` as used by `app/api/feed/music/route.ts:18-21` - are unchanged by this file.

`idx_artist_music_trust_status_idx` and `idx_artist_music_certification_status_idx` from `20260910140000:47-52` already cover the base table and are untouched. The news feed's music select does not filter on the trust columns, so no index is warranted for them here.
constraintsAndIndexes.validationPlan: The file's own post-condition DO block is the target-side validation, and it is proven able to FAIL in the three ways that matter, measured by executing the extracted block standalone against a deliberately broken state: (1) with the view replaced by the chain's own 34-column definition, it raised `public.music_tracks resolves to 34 output columns, expected 38`; (2) with a 39-column view carrying an extra output column, it raised `resolves to 39 output columns, expected 38`; (3) with `security_invoker` reset, it raised `missing security_invoker=true (reloptions: )`. Controls 1 and 2 were each preceded by an explicit fixture assertion that the view really had 34 and 39 columns, because the first revision of control 1 was VACUOUS: it used `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` to restore a 34-column view, which PostgreSQL refuses with 42P13, so the view was never actually changed and the gate read green against an untouched fixture. That is the fourth time in this repository's recent history that a control exercised nothing - the lesson recorded in DB-013 and DB-014 STATE entries is that a control must assert its own post-state, and this one now does. Each control was followed by a re-apply, which returned the block to GREEN except where the 39-column case correctly stays red. A committed contract-test `.sql` file is NOT provided: `supabase/tests/` is outside DB-019's working set. The repository's existing `supabase/tests/db008_view_column_replay.harness.sh` covers the complementary direction - it resolves this view's real SELECT list on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16 and compares it with the contract in both directions - and after this file it will report `viewOnlyColumns=4` on its INFO line, which is the expected and correct consequence.

recovery.rollback: `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW public.music_tracks AS <the 34-column definition from 20260711165607:119-153>;` issued as a LATER FORWARD MIGRATION, never as an edit to this file. Rolling back is a four-column REMOVAL, which the replace form can express because it is a truncation of columns this file itself appended - PostgreSQL permits removing trailing columns the same way it permits appending them. Rolling back also means the news feed's music section goes back to being empty on PostgREST 400, which is the state every deployed environment is in today; it is a truthful regression, not a new one, and the operator should say so in the release ticket rather than shipping the rollback quietly. `ALTER VIEW public.music_tracks RESET (security_invoker)` is NOT part of the rollback: that reloption predates this file and removing it would be a data-disclosure change.
recovery.forwardFix: Any correction is a new additive migration with a higher version carrying another `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`. Two shapes are already anticipated by this file's post-condition, so a bad forward fix cannot be applied silently: a wrong output-column count and a missing `security_invoker` both RAISE. A forward fix cannot accidentally narrow the view either, because PostgreSQL refuses a replacement that drops an existing output column before this file's post-condition is ever reached. Note the ordering constraint this creates: a forward fix may only APPEND, never remove, so a column this file adds cannot later be retired by a replacement view - it needs its own migration and a deliberate decision about the four consumers that would have to stop reading it first.
